#6471. Are Uranus and Neptune Secretly "Rock Giants"? A Noble Gas Might Hold the Answer

For decades, astronomers have divided the planets in the outer solar system into two distinct camps. Jupiter and Saturn were the âgas giantsâ made up primarily of hydrogen and helium. Uranus and Neptune were the âice giantsâ, and were much smaller but were packed with heavier elements. A new paper from Olivier Mousis of the Southwest Research Institute and his co-authors, available in The Planetary Science Journal, explores whether we can use an isotope of a noble gas - argon-40 - to determine whether there are hidden mountains of rock under the ice giantâs thick atmospheres.

Scientists are getting excited because there has been an ongoing debate that these distant worlds are actually covered in rock. But we canât simply fly a probe out a few billion miles and drill down into their surfaces to determine that for ourselves. Instead, they decided to use proxies, such as the concentration of argon-40, as a rough measurement for how much rock there is below the atmosphere.

Understanding why the presence of one noble gas isotope leads to understanding whether rock is present or not requires a bit of a diversion into the world of bananas. Or at least, it gives me an excuse to talk about bananas in a planetary science article. Bananas are radioactive, and the thing causing their radioactivity is potassium-40 - a relatively unstable form of a very common element. When potassium-40 decays, it turns into argon-40, which, as a noble gas, hardly interacts with anything.

Fraser talks about how to plan a mission to Uranus.

Most of this radioactive decay takes place in rocks containing potassium-40, rather than bananas, so one of the most common sources of argon-40 is literally rocks. After it is created, it bubbles up out of those rocks and escapes into its host planetâs atmosphere. In fact, it makes up around 1% of the air youâre breathing right now.

On the ice giants, this same process could hold - argon-40 could form inside a rocky surface, and then bubble up into the planetâs atmosphere over billions of years. So we should be able to send a probe to measure the concentration of argon-40 in their atmospheres, and that would serve as an effective proxy for the existence of rock under the atmosphere.

Thereâs just one catch - rocks arenât really the only source of argon-40. In fact, there was already plenty of it floating around in the protosolar nebula that the Sun and all the planets eventually formed out of. Therefore, Uranus and Neptune could have âtrappedâ this leftover argon-40 before they were even mature, causing argon-40 to eventually appear in their atmosphere, but not from rocky surfaces.

Fraser talks about efforts to go back to visit the ice giants of the solar system.

According to the paper, the amount of argon collected by the early versions of Neptune and Uranus depends entirely on where they formed with regards to the âargon ice lineâ. This line, which happens around 23-35 Kelvin, the temperature that argon freezes into solid ice, or is trapped inside water ice, is the determining factor of how much primordial argon Neptune and Uranus had sucked up.

Unfortunately, thereâs still a lot of debate about where exactly in the solar system the ice giants formed. If they formed close to the Sun and eventually migrated back out to the edges of the solar system, they might not have captured much argon ice, and the majority of the argon in their atmospheres would be due to release from rocks. On the other hand, if the theories about them actively moving through the solar system soon after their creation are true, then they would likely have captured a large amount of argon-40, making it useless as an indicator of whether or not the planets have a rocky surface.

Luckily, there is a way to potentially solve this puzzle. Argon-40 has a lighter isotopic cousin, known as argon-36, which is non-radioactive, and doesnât form in decaying rocks. Measuring its level would act like a control group, allowing scientists to estimate how much of the argon present in the atmosphere would have been swallowed at birth, as we have other estimates of the ratio between argon-40 and argon-36 in the early solar system.

Itâs good these sorts of insights are coming out now, as there is currently a mission, Uranus Orbiter and Probe, which is in active development and planned to arrive in the system in the 2040s. That still gives us some time to finalize our theories about what we would expect to find there. And perhaps, once it does arrive, weâll be able to definitively answer whether or not the âIce giantsâ have a truly solid surface or not.

SwRI - SwRI team studies interior composition, origins of ice giants

UT - Argon â The First Noble Gas Molecules Discovered In Space

#6470. The Absolute Best Pie Recipes, According to Eater Staff

The dessert course is about to go off with a perfect pumpkin pie, chocolate peanut butter pie, a caramelized onion tart, and more

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

You don’t really need a holiday occasion to bake a pie, but it doesn’t hurt to let the spirit of the season introduce you to a few more festive recipes. Whether you’re a fan of savory dishes, prefer fruit pies, or love the wobble of a perfectly set custard pie, there is a pie for everyone — including Eater staffers.

We love a super-easy no-bake pie just as much as we love a more complex, picture-perfect creation. Here are some of our favorite pie recipes to make at home this holiday season and beyond.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Since I grew up in Los Angeles and had never heard of buttermilk pie, it may come as a surprise that it’s one of my go-to pies to make. I discovered it seven years ago on a Twitter thread about unique, regional pies and was fascinated enough by this classic Southern dessert to attempt it, trying the first recipe that came up on my Google search. This is that recipe, and it has been consistently easy and perfect since that very first pie I made. The filling is smooth and velvety with subtle notes of nutmeg and a kiss of lemon. It reminds me of dan tat, or Chinese egg tarts, but it’s way less fussy. Yes, you can make your own pie crust, but storebought works well here, too, because the real star is the wobbly buttermilk custard. — Kat Thompson, audience editor

When fall comes around, I turn to this tried and true caramelized onion and butternut squash tart from Food 52 over and over again. It’s a perfect savory option to bring to Friendsgiving, Thanksgiving, or any autumnal get together. What I love most about it is that it highlights flavors and ingredients of the season while standing out from the plentiful pumpkin and pecan pies that you’re sure to find at any gathering. To make it heartier, I sometimes add crumbled sausage to the mix. — Terri Ciccone, deputy director of audience development

The only thing my mom and I love more than re-invigorating this incredibly simple chess pie recipe is telling the (most likely made up) story behind the name. Trying on my grandmother’s Texas twang, we explain how a server at a diner was once asked the flavor of the custard pie that day. She said, “It’s just pie,” but with her Southern accent that was mistaken as “chess pie.” And so we got this simple custard pie, which is filled with evaporated milk and set perfectly with cornmeal. My mom started experimenting with adding edible lavender oil to the recipe, which has became my favorite way to bake it, but she’s also added a tablespoon or two of my dad’s “Mexican mocha” (spiced hot chocolate) mix to make an incredible chocolate custard pie with a kick. But even plain, this pie recipe is always a big hit. — Emily Venezky, social media manager

I have nothing but the utmost respect for people who lovingly make intricately crafted, high-maintenance pies with lattice crusts and the whole shebang, but my personal tried-and-true, always-go-back pie recipe is one I’ve frequently revisited since high school: no-bake chocolate peanut butter pie. I do not know the true origin of the semi-homemade, Sandra Lee-esque creation, but if you stumble upon some version of the five-ish-ingredient recipe that includes Cool Whip, like this one on the blog Crazy for Crust, that’s what I’m referring to. Rest assured that I generally have the taste and standards of a bougie person, but this extremely simple, absolutely-not-healthy recipe is just perfection. It’s sweet, salty, creamy, and simultaneously light, fluffy, rich, and decadent. Whenever I make it for a dinner party, holiday gathering, or potluck, it garners rave reviews (the word “orgasmic” has been used to describe it more than once). And as a child of the ‘90s, I love using an Oreo crust and Skippy peanut butter — forever crowd-pleasers. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor

“We have Milk Bar at home, honey” is what comes to mind whenever I make this pie, which reminds me of the New York City bakery’s famous, albeit once salaciously named dessert (now called the Milk Bar Pie). This butterscotch pie from Smitten Kitchen packs the same gooey, buttery taste and a satisfyingly sticky consistency — I feel like it’s a pie for people who wish they could just eat caramelized graham cracker crusts and custards for dessert. — Francky Knapp, staff writer

This zingy citrus pie might evoke summertime, but that’s exactly why I make sure it’s on the table during the holidays. Somewhere between a lemon pie and an icebox pudding, Atlantic Beach Pie delivers the bracing acidity I crave after a marathon of rich food. It originated at a North Carolina seafood restaurant, acting as a clever loophole to the old wives’ tale that eating dessert after a seafood meal could be deadly. Believe the lore or not, this pie is bound to earn seconds, whether for its salty, buttery saltine crust, zippy custard filling, or cloud of velvety whipped cream. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director

Claudia Fleming, adapted by Amanda Hesser for the New York Times

I am not a pie person, per se — I hate the pressure of making a flaky crust — but I don’t mind the less-stress approach of making a tart, which asks only that I press dough into a tart pan. This famous chocolate caramel tart, a version of which my mom made frequently when I was growing up, is a dish I would definitely have on my roster if Mythical Kitchen ever invited me onto Last Meals. With dark chocolate ganache, a caramel filling that’s made more complex by the addition of salt and creme fraiche, and a sprinkling of a little more flaky salt on top, it tastes like a slightly more sophisticated Twix Bar.

I once asked my mom to make it for an ex-boyfriend, with me talking it up to him as my favorite dessert ever, and when he told me it was “just okay” — and who says that, especially when presented with a free dessert that required the dessert-giver to make a caramel? — that was the final sign I needed that he was not the one for me. Lesson learned: My husband and I are very dessert-compatible. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

#6469. A Chemical Signature Suddenly Disappeared From Earth’s Rocks. Scientists Think They Know Why

Scientists have uncovered a mysterious chemical change in ancient rocks that reveals a major turning point in Earth’s geological history.

A chemical fingerprint preserved in some of Earth’s oldest rocks disappears from the geological record around 2.5 billion years ago. Researchers at Curtin University have traced this abrupt change across thousands of rock samples, identifying a major transition in how Earth’s crust formed and recycled. Their findings suggest that the planet was beginning to develop a tectonic system resembling the one operating today.

Determining when plate tectonics emerged has been a longstanding challenge. The movement of Earth’s tectonic plates continually reshapes continents and ocean basins, while recycling enormous amounts of crust into the planet’s interior. This process destroys much of the geological evidence needed to reconstruct its earliest history.

The researchers investigated chemical signatures that can survive when older crust melts and contributes to the formation of new rock. These signatures can help identify the original material from which younger rocks formed.

“New crust often forms by melting older rock, leaving behind a distinctive chemical fingerprint,” said lead author Dr. Janne Liebmann, a research fellow at Curtin University. “We searched for this fingerprint in thousands of rocks from around the world, spanning almost four billion years of Earth’s history.”

“We found it consistently in rocks older than 2.5 billion years, showing they were derived from a pool of ancient crust that formed about four billion years ago.”

“But after 2.5 billion years ago, that fingerprint disappears from the geological record, and despite examining thousands of rocks, we never see it again.”

The disappearance suggests that the processes responsible for generating new crust underwent a fundamental transformation. Rather than repeatedly melting and reworking ancient crust in place, Earth increasingly developed a system capable of transporting and recycling crust across much larger distances.

“That tells us something fundamental changed in the way Earth’s crust was being formed and transformed, marking a transition towards the dynamic tectonic system we see today,” Liebmann said.

Study co-author Professor Chris Kirkland, from Curtin’s School of Earth and Planetary Sciences, connected the findings to the geological processes that distinguish Earth from planets such as Venus and Mars, which lack a comparable global system of active plate tectonics.

“Plate tectonics is fundamental to the way Earth has evolved over billions of years, continually reshaping the continents and oceans and influencing the planet’s atmosphere and climate,” Kirkland said.

“What makes this finding remarkable is that we can see the fingerprints of an ancient Earth disappear from the geological record at a very specific point in time.”

“It marks the transition from an early Earth where ancient crust could be repeatedly melted and reworked in place, to a system capable of moving and recycling crust on a much larger scale.”

The results identify a major change in crustal evolution around 2.5 billion years ago, although they do not establish that modern plate tectonics began suddenly or that all its defining features emerged simultaneously.

“This gives us our clearest geological evidence yet for when the tectonic engine that drives the modern Earth ‘switched on’.”

Reference: “Loss of ancient crustal reservoirs marks a shift in Earth’s geodynamic regime” by Janne Liebmann, Christopher L. Kirkland, Michael I. H. Hartnady and Christopher J. Spencer, 1 November 2026, Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences. DOI: 10.1098/rspa.2026.0587

Recently, researchers used AI to "decode" segments of birdsong. In the wake of this, Live Science asks its readers which animal they'd want to communicate with.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The idea of talking to animals like Dr. Dolittle might sound far-fetched, but researchers are making progress toward understanding how other species communicate. In a recent Live Science interview, University of California, Berkeley ethologist Julie Elie explained how she used artificial intelligence (AI) and behavioral experiments to decode the calls of zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata). For instance, Elie was able to determine which calls the birds used to communicate over short distances versus longer distances.

Birds aren't the only animals scientists are hoping to understand. Researchers with Project CETI are using AI to decipher the clicks and calls of sperm whales, while a separate team (with the search for extraterrestrial intelligence, or SETI) conducted what they described as the first "conversation" between humans and a humpback whale. The whale, named Twain, responded to recorded calls played by researchers over a 20 minute period, a "conversation" scientists believe could help us figure out how to communicate with extraterrestrial life someday.

Closer to home, cats have already figured out how to use meows to get their human's attention, whether they're demanding food, affection or simply that we open the door for them (again). Whether this means they understand the human language or not is still up for debate, but it raises an interesting question: If we could understand what animals were saying, which species would you most want to talk to? Vote in our poll and let us know what you'd ask in the comments below!

#6467. The Simons Observatory is Online and Surveying the Cosmic Microwave Background

The Simons Observatory in the Atacama Desert has begun its mission to survey the Cosmic Microwave Background. Its goal is to detect undeniable evidence of the Big Bang and cosmic inflation. Can this unique survey succeed where others have failed?

We live in an age of large astronomical surveys, enabled by powerful computers and data handling methods. While powerful telescopes still perform detailed observations of individual targets, and always will, wide surveys have a power all their own. The ESA's Gaia mission, for example, has completed its survey of billions of stars and generated a massive amount of foundational data that researchers will draw on for decades to come.

There are automated surveys for transients like supernovae and asteroids, radio-sky surveys to spot objects obscured by thick dust, and massive surveys just getting started like the Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's three core surveys.

But another Simons Observatory's survey hasn't garnered the same attention that some of the other have. The Simons Observatory (SO) consists of four telescopes working together: three small 0.5 meter aperture 'scopes in its Small Aperture Telescope (SAT) and one large 6-meter one in its Large Aperture Telescope (LAT).

The unusual configuration gives the SO the best chance to observe tiny details in the Universe's first observable light, the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB).

This image of the Cosmic Microwave Background is from the Simons Observatory, the newest and most powerful observatory to study the CMB. It's unique arrangement of three small and one large telescope increases its resolution by an order of magnitude over its predecessor, the Planck satellite. The Simons Observatory's main goal is to find the elusive evidence from the epoch of inflation, and thereby confirming the Big Bang model of cosmology. Image Credit: Simons Observatory.

The stuff of the Universe was too opaque for light to travel through it at first. Photons were effectively scattered by the hot, dense plasma that permeated the Universe. Eventually conditions changed. The Universe expanded, the plasma cooled, and photons could travel. This was the recombination epoch and it occurred about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.

Note that the name is historical and reflected our earlier understanding of the Universe. It wasn't actually a recombination, it was the first time that electrons and protons combined to form neutral hydrogen, and that's what made the cosmos transparent. Its name should probably be changed to the combination epoch.

But regardless of its name, the cosmic microwave background is the relic radiation from the Universe's first light, and it holds clues to the Universe, especially to the Big Bang theory of cosmology.

Other efforts have been made to map the CMB. NASA's Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) and the ESA's Planck satellite both made the effort from orbit. Currently, the South Pole Telescope (SPT) and related facilities are doing the same.

The SPT made an important discovery. It detected for the first time what's called the B-mode polarization of the CMB. The B-mode is important because it was created by primordial gravitational waves generated during the epoch of inflation, the first moments of the Universe's inflation. So finding the B-mode was important evidence for the Big Bang theory.

The South Pole Telescope at the AmundsenâScott South Pole Station, Antarctica. The SPT is a 10-meter telescope that is credited with the first detection of the Cosmic Microwave Background's B-mode polarization. Image Credit: By Amble - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/9057466

But there was a problem. Gravitational lensing can also create B-mode polarization, and it has nothing to do with the Big Bang or inflation. It's difficult to tell which source created the B-mode polarization the SPT detected. So its initial detection was put in doubt.

This is where the Simons Observatory comes into the picture. It's been calibrating its instruments for two years and is now getting down to business.

âTo have all the observatory motors humming, gears turning and data flowing makes me joyful, but even more exciting is the prospect of what we could find in its big new deep and detailed maps,â says Simons Observatory Co-Director Suzanne Staggs of Princeton University.

This time-lapse shows the Simons Observatory's Large Area Telescope scanning the sky in August 2026. Credit: David Boettger

The observatory's four telescopes collectively have tens of thousands of microwave detectors, almost 98,000 of them. That's 16 times more than one of its predecessors, the Atacama Cosmology Telescope. They're not only mapping the CMB the same way that WMAP and the Planck satellite did. They're also searching for the tiny fluctuations in the CMB, the B-mode polarizations that can confirm the Big Bang and cosmic inflation. If detected, the SO can determine if these are true artifacts of primordial gravitational waves, or artifacts of the polluting gravitational lensing that confounded the SPT.

It'll take years of observations before that can be achieved, but the SO's first observations are already showing the observatory's power. Its sensitivity is meant to be an order of magnitude highter than its predecessor, the Planck satellite. âThe images that weâve made with just a few months of data are already deeper and less noisy than Planckâs, which were collected over years,â says Simons Observatory Spokesperson Jo Dunkley of Princeton University. That's significant, because the Planck outperformed its predecessor, WMAP, and is considered the benchmark for CMB observations. So the SO is already establishing a new benchmark for observations.

The SO's unique four telescope design is already showing its value. The large, 6-meter telescope is able to observe more of the sky in higher resolution than other CMB telescopes. Every couple of days, it scans half of the available sky.

âIt is incredibly satisfying to see the early maps, knowing that our initial data places us at the forefront of the field â and that we are poised to go much further,â says Jeffrey McMahon, observatory testing lead at the University of Chicago.

The SO isn't isolated and alone in its work. All of these CMB surveys and observatories will work together in the end. For example, the SPT and other facilities at its site are mapping gravitational lenses that can interfere with the detection of B-modes from primordial gravitational waves in the epoch of inflation. Those templates can be used to help remove their pollution from CMB surveys. So it's all hands on deck.

This cut-away schematic shows the Large Area Telescope's Receiver with one of its optical tubes highlighted. Note the pulse tube coolers and the dilution refrigerator. They keep the telescope at the cryogenic temperatures necessary for microwave observations. Image Credit: Simons Observatory/Nicholas Galitzki et al. 2018. Conference Proceedings.

The SO is an observer of polarized light, and that means that while its primary goal is searching for B-mode polarization, its maps have other things to reveal, too. âThere are a number of large surveys adding to our understanding of the universe,â Staggs says. âOur idea is that we can combine our data with theirs to further our discoveries.â

This is especially true of other wide surveys like the Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time. The pair will create a potent combination for detecting transients across multiple wavelengths. âThe instrument is now sensitive enough that we can see small changes in transients in only a few days, whereas ACT took months,â Devlin says. âThis enables us to observe entirely new classes of objects.â Its science observations have barely begun, and it's already giant stellar flares and asteroids in the Milky Way, and activity around a supermassive black holes outside of our galaxy.

But detecting that elusive evidence from the epoch of inflation is the SO's holy grail, and if it finds it, it will be a collective finding in the mass data the observatory will produce. Like other survey telescopes, the data will be released in large sequential data releases.

âWeâll be providing everything to the community through a data management tool, which we hope to have completed for the first data release,â Devlin says.

The initial success of its first science operations is a hopeful indication that it can finally find the evidence of cosmic inflation, the B-mode polarization from primordial gravitational waves in the CMB.

âEssentially, right out of the box, just turning on the instrument, weâre making beautiful crisp images of the Milky Way,â Staggs says. Those images are uncovering new observations of the galaxy's magnetic fields, and understanding them is critical to understanding star formation and how the galaxy evolves.

âThis moment marks a major milestone in our effort to understand these big questions about the universe,â Devlin says. âI think thereâs going to be so many scientific discoveries coming out in the next few years, itâll be hard to keep up.â

The SO's performance will improve when another three small telescopes are added in 2027. That will also double the Small Area Telescope's number of individual detectors to 48,160 detectors. The original five-year survey has been extended, too.

"Combined with a planned extension of the survey duration to 2035, this expansion will significantly enhance SO's search for a B-mode signal in the polarisation of the cosmic microwave background, a potential signature of gravitational waves produced in the very early Universe," explain the authors of a 2026 paper in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics.

#6466. Jim Jordan picked as new minority leader for House GOP

Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, center, arrives for a House Republican leadership candidate forum for the 120th Congress in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday, with Rep. Celeste Maloy, R-Utah, walking alongside him. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Republicans on Tuesday opted for a new face atop their ranks, electing Rep. Jim Jordan as the incoming minority leader for the 120th Congress after Republicans suffered massive losses in last week’s midterm elections.

The Ohio Republican defeated outgoing Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., in a closed-door, secret-ballot election. The final tally was 106-73.

“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. Democrats offer more government. We will offer more freedom,” Jordan said after the hourslong process.

The two had been working the phones before making their pitches during a candidates forum in the Capitol Visitor Center’s auditorium on Tuesday morning. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced last week he would not seek a leadership post in the new Congress, which will be seated on Jan. 3.

“Obviously Jim and I know each other, but I’ve got a proven record of how to bring people together,” Scalise said ahead of the vote, trying to play up his experience, including more than a decade on the leadership team that included a stint as whip.

As House Republicans trickled out of the candidates’ forum for breaks or to take phone calls, one member, granted anonymity to discuss a private session, said Scalise and Jordan “both have strong points, but they both have flaws.” Each made an unsuccessful bid for speaker in 2023 after the ouster of Kevin McCarthy, before the gavel ultimately went to Johnson.

Declining to reveal which would get his vote, the member said: “I won’t talk about a secret vote, but I know who I think is best to lead us.”

The incoming minority conference also selected other leaders on Tuesday.

Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota held off a challenge from Texas Rep. August Pfluger to become minority whip in January, despite some grumbling about how tight votes were handled on the floor this year.

“We’ve got to retool our whip operation,” Texas Rep. Nathaniel Moran said Tuesday morning, pointing to “the number of times we were held up by either discharge petitions or failed rule votes.”

“Those were things that should not have happened in the majority,” said Moran as he publicly backed Pfluger for whip.

But Emmer projected confidence after his whip win, comparing the moment to when Republicans were down and out after their losses in 2018 only to rebound a few years later.

“To our colleagues on the left, enjoy this honeymoon phase, because come Jan. 3, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot,” he said at a news conference, adding that Republicans under his watch would expose the “empty promises” that Democrats made to voters and push back on what he called their “radical” agenda.

In the day’s only three-way race, conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan defeated Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida to keep her spot.

“We had a spirited leadership election. There were important conversations about the future of our conference, and I listened,” McClain said at the news conference.

In the race to lead House Republicans’ campaign arm, Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia defeated Rep. Rudy Yakym of Indiana, seen as an up-and-coming Ways and Means Committee member. That means Jack will take on a huge share of the uphill task of selecting candidates and raising funds for the 2028 cycle as he helms the National Republican Congressional Committee.

But most of the attention heading into Tuesday’s closed-door proceedings was on the minority leader race.

Johnson, the outgoing speaker, declined to endorse a candidate but had encouraging words for Jordan after his win. “He’s going to do an excellent job. He’s a good, trusted friend and brother,” he said.

Rep. Tom Cole, R-Okla., said it was a “tough choice for the conference to make,” but he wasn’t disappointed in the pick. “He was an exceptionally capable chairman of both Oversight and Judiciary. He’s excellent in an interview,” Cole said of Jordan. “He’s got boundless energy and determination.”

Jordan’s victory means he will form a political and legal tag team with newly installed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller in pushing back on a number of investigations House Democrats have planned for President Donald Trump, some of his second-term administration officials and his business-minded family members.

Democrats will have more than 250 seats in the chamber, with a number of races still uncalled. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, expected to become the next House speaker, told reporters last week he predicts Democrats will have at least 255 seats when all the ballots have been counted and verification processes have played out.

“It’s a historic majority in the 21st century,” Jeffries told reporters in Washington, D.C., the day after the midterms. “The American people have chosen the economy over extremism. The American people have chosen hope over hatred. The American people have chosen common sense over corruption, chaos and cruelty. The American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction.”

Political analysts have predicted an internal battle within the GOP for the direction the party takes over the next two years — and after Trump leaves office in January 2029.

The Institute for Legislative Analysis, a nonprofit organization that advocates to shrink the size and influence of the government, released a vote study assessment on Monday. Its calculations led ILA to endorse Emmer and three fresh faces: Jordan, Steube and Jack.

“It’s clear many Republican voters feel their representatives in Washington aren’t representing them,” Ryan McGowan, the institute’s CEO, said in a statement. “It will be interesting to see whether House Republicans respond by choosing leaders … whose voting records are much more closely aligned with the party’s conservative base.”

Several GOP sources late last week, granted anonymity to be candid, said they were expecting a close outcome between Scalise and Jordan, adding Emmer was working the phones hard to remain whip. One said having either Scalise or Jordan atop the conference, with the expectation of Emmer staying on as whip, “won’t be much of a change at the top.”

The new leadership team will take over Jan. 3, when Democrats are expected to, in part, use their large majority to target all things Trump 2.0. The same GOP source said the majority party will “inevitably be pursuing impeachment by August recess despite their disciplined statements to the media pre-election.”

Trump replied in the affirmative when a “60 Minutes” correspondent asked him in an interview that aired Sunday night if he could work with Democrats, should they also be aggressively investigating his team.

“Well, I did it for four years,” the president said of his first term. “They impeached me twice. And there are those that say that worked out to my advantage.”

Nina Heller, Michael Macagnone and Samantha Freeman contributed to this report.

#6464. Reconstructing Cosmic History and Earth's Evolution From Cosmic Explosions

When we think of the Solar System, we often view it as a self-contained entity, isolated from its cosmic neighborhood. However, scientists have long known that the planets of the Solar System are subject to activity in nearby star systems, including supernovae and other energetic astrophysical events. For example, it is established that intermediate elements and the heaviest elements on the periodic table are created when stars reach the end of their life cycle and explode, sending their outer layers (with these elements) into space.

These include intermediate elements ranging from carbon and oxygen to iron, nickel, and radioactive isotopes thereof, as well as heavy elements like zinc, silver, tin, gold, mercury, lead, platinum, and uranium. At the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR), Prof. Anton Wallner and his team have launched the SUPREME project to uncover traces of these elements. Their goal is to use them to reconstruct the history of cosmic events in our neighborhood and shed light on how the heaviest elements are created in nature.

The project was recently awarded a â¬3 million grant ($3.29 million USD) through the European Research Council's (ERC) Advanced Grants program. Prof. Wallner and his team were one of 319 leading research groups across Europe selected for funding totaling â¬838 million ($918.86 million USD) to pursue projects that could lead to major scientific breakthroughs. The SUPREME project aims to address two fundamental questions in modern astrophysics, focusing on the past 500 million years.

First, there's the question of how nearby supernovae have affected Earth and biological evolution since the Cambrian Period (ca. 538.8 to 485 million years ago), the geological era that coincided with the rapid explosion of complex marine life (aka. the Cambrian Explosion). When the Cambrian began, the continents were largely located in the southern hemisphere and were mostly barren. But as the period progressed and gave way to subsequent geological eras, life began to emerge from the oceans, giving rise to plants, mammals, dinosaurs, and eventually primates.

Supernovae, when they happen in our cosmic neighborhood, distribute heavy elements like gold, platinum, lead, and zinc to Earth. Credit: NASA

Second, there's the question of how the heaviest elements in the Universe are created and distributed; in this case, to the Earth and Moon. To answer these questions, researchers at the SUPREME project will search for extremely rare radioactive isotopes in lunar samples provided by NASA, deep-sea sediments, ice cores, and other geological archives. These archives preserve the history of interstellar material that arrived on Earth over eons, allowing scientists to identify and date nearby supernovae and other nearby energetic events.

Their work will build on the first detection of radioactive isotopes created by a rapid neutron-capture (r-process) event in history, the process by which about half of all atoms heavier than iron are created in the Universe. This occured in June 2026, when scientists from the HZDR made the first significant measurement of curium-247 and plutonium-244 in interstellar matter trapped on Earth. As Prof. Sebastian M. Schmidt, the Scientific Director of HZDR who led the discovery team, said in an HZDR statement:

This award is a remarkable recognition of Anton Wallner's internationally leading research. SUPREME addresses fundamental questions about the origin of the elements and the history of our cosmic environment while building on measurement capabilities that are unique worldwide. We are proud that this pioneering work is being carried out at HZDR.

To detect and measure rare radioactive isotopes, the researchers will use HAMSTER (Helmholtz Accelerator Mass Spectrometer Tracing Environmental Radionuclides), a new state-of-the-art accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) facility developed by Wallner and his team and installed at HZDR in 2025. Combined with an innovative laser-based technology that dramatically reduces measurement background, the team will be able to detect individual atoms with unprecedented sensitivity, opening new possibilities for astrophysics and other scientific applications.

The results of this project are expected to provide unprecedented insights into the history of our cosmic neighborhood and its possible influence on Earth's geology and species evolution. "Securing one of the European Union's most competitive research grants is an outstanding accomplishment," said Saxony's Minister of Science, Sebastian Gemkow. "This distinction is not only a major milestone in the recipients' scientific careers, but also a significant gain for Saxony as a leading research and innovation hub."

Matt Williams is a space journalist, science communicator, and author with several published titles and studies. His work is featured in The Ross 248 Project and Interstellar Travel edited by NASA alumni Les Johnson and Ken Roy. He also hosts the podcast series Stories from Space on Patreon. He lives in beautiful British Columbia with his wife and family. For more information, check out his website.

#6463. A Century-Old Pollution Disaster Has Been Discovered Frozen in Arctic Ice

Decisions made at one Montana smelter may have shaped the air millions breathed, while Arctic ice reveals how much pollution earlier controls could have prevented.

More than a century ago, toxic pollution from a copper smelter in Montana was spreading across North America, reaching communities thousands of miles from its source. Much of that contamination went unmeasured at the time, but traces of it survived in an unexpected place: Arctic ice.

Scientists have now used those frozen records to uncover how one industrial operation may have exposed millions of people to harmful levels of arsenic and lead. The findings also demonstrate how the Earth’s ice preserves evidence of human activity long after pollution has disappeared from the air.

The study, published November 10 in Nature Sustainability, was led by Joe McConnell and Nathan Chellman of the Desert Research Institute (DRI), alongside international collaborators. The team examined 10 ice cores from Greenland, northern Canada, and the Russian Arctic, finding that concentrations of toxic metals in some locations rose to approximately 15 times preindustrial levels between 1886 and 1918.

The evidence pointed to the Anaconda Copper Mine complex near Butte, Montana, one of the world’s largest copper producers at the time. Researchers estimated that during its peak production decades, the operation released approximately 11,000 tons of arsenic and 4,400 tons of lead into the atmosphere each year.

“It’s pretty wild to think that a single, albeit massive source of pollution could have affected effectively the entire North American continent and western Greenland more than 4000 kilometers or 2500 miles away,” McConnell said.

Using historical census records and models of atmospheric pollution, the researchers estimated that approximately 50.5 million Americans and 600,000 Canadians were exposed to arsenic concentrations associated with increased risks of lung cancer and other serious illnesses.

People living near the operation faced particularly high exposure. For nearly 30 years, residents of Montana and parts of Wyoming and Idaho experienced arsenic concentrations that met or exceeded the World Health Organization’s current recommended maximum threshold for chronic exposure. The researchers also estimated that 1.4 million Americans and Canadians encountered elevated lead pollution potentially associated with cognitive effects equivalent to a 2.6-point reduction in IQ.

Although the study did not directly measure health outcomes, arsenic and lead exposure are associated with cancer, diabetes, cognitive decline, and heart disease. Pollution settling onto crops, soil, and water could also have created additional risks beyond those examined in the study.

To reconstruct this forgotten pollution, scientists turned to the Arctic’s natural record of atmospheric change. As snow accumulates, it traps tiny particles carried by the wind, including industrial pollutants. Over time, the snow becomes ice, preserving chemical evidence of conditions from decades or even centuries earlier.

By comparing metal concentrations across the 10 ice cores, combining them with atmospheric models, and examining historical mining records, the researchers traced the contamination to northern North America. Arsenic measurements, supported by related chemical markers, closely matched Anaconda’s production history, while lead isotope evidence reinforced the connection.

The timing also revealed how industrial decisions shaped the atmosphere. Copper demand surged during rapid electrification and the buildup to World War I, increasing pollution from ore processing. Near Anaconda, damaged crops, reduced harvests, and livestock deaths had already prompted decades of legal disputes.

After the company installed pollution-control equipment around 1919, heavy-metal emissions declined by approximately 65%, according to the ice-core evidence. Similar technology had been available years earlier, but Anaconda delayed installation for roughly a decade.

The researchers calculated that installing those controls ten years sooner could have prevented another 60,000 tons of arsenic and 24,000 tons of lead from spreading across much of North America.

The Arctic record captures both sides of that history. It reveals how pollution from one industrial site reached millions of people and how changes in industrial practices eventually reduced its impact. Even today, the ice preserves evidence of environmental damage that otherwise might have remained largely hidden.

Reference: “Widespread North American pollution and health impacts from early twentieth century copper production” by Joseph R. McConnell, Nathan J. Chellman, Sophie M. Wensman, Alison S. Criscitiello, Andreas Plach, Dorthe Dahl-Jensen, Diedrich Fritzsche, Kira M. Holland, Drake McCrimmon, Matthew B. Osman, John Sandlos and Andreas Stohl, 10 November 2026, Nature Sustainability. DOI: 10.1038/s41893-026-01975-9

#6462. The Best Thanksgiving Side Recipes, According to Eater Editors

With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table

The sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument. Mashed potatoes and stuffing are the reason we’re all convening at the table, right? Aaaaand the whole “gathering with loved ones” thing too, of course.

While we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever new ideas have been simmering since last year’s big meal. They’re our chance to create a menu with balance, adding a bright, crunchy salad that perfectly offsets the richness of all those buttery potatoes or offering an essential hit of cozy baked pasta with melty cheese.

These are the Thanksgiving sides recipes that Eater editors have vetted as being worth the space on our holiday tables.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Every year, my sister and I have a stuffing-off. Not that we’re all that competitive (we are), but she insists on having her signature mushroom and sage stuffing, and I insist on making the best stuffing. My recipe is just an old Gourmet magazine version of sausage cornbread stuffing with a bunch of fennel, but what makes it exceptional is my own riff on what is so often overlooked as filler when it comes to stuffing (or, depending on where you’re from, dressing): the bread cubes. I take the full loaves of Whole Foods’ signature cornbread, slice them into cubes, stick them in a low oven (around 200 degrees) for a few hours, and eureka! It’s a stuffing that delivers again and again.

Why are the store-bought loaves the key? I’m not quite sure. My hunch is that they’re just dense enough, un-fresh enough, and mass-produced enough to dry out easily, and the store’s recipe strikes some unicorn balance of flavor that compliments the fennel without making the dish overwhelmingly sweet. — Lesley Suter, brand director

I keep coming back to this deeply savory, unexpected side dish when the weather turns cold. Its varying textures, ample acidity, and subtle sweetness are a welcome addition to any spread of holiday sides. Cabbage and bacon might be a familiar pairing, but the miso paste and Dijon that are swirled into the reduction offer a pleasant and welcome surprise to the palate. An added bonus: Jesse’s videos are some of the most relaxing and soul-soothing I’ve seen on the internet; it’s as if he invented food ASMR himself. Let them regulate your blood pressure this holiday season when that one in-law’s antics start to send you over the edge. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director

Nobody says they crave a salad at Thanksgiving, but I promise you they do, especially once the heaviness of everything else starts to set in. At the very least, I crave a salad at Thanksgiving, and the kind of salad I desire in an instance like this is something crunchy and bright and which tastes nothing like anything else on the table. Thus, some combination of citrus and fennel is generally my go-to. The citrus lends a brightness that pairs well with the cranberry sauce that’s inevitably on my plate, and I like the licorice sweetness of fennel amid the savoriness that dominates the spread; plus, I think it goes well with the celery that’s in other dishes.

While more complex takes on this kind of salad exist and sound delicious, I find the most pared-down versions easier to slot into my day of cooking. This salad is usually my very last task before we sit down to eat. Sometimes, I don’t even announce that it’s happening, so it seems like the “just threw this together,” afterthought touch that surprises you with how essential it ends up being. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

Tauba Auerbach, Salad for President by Julia Sherman

Tauba Auerbach’s Brussels sprouts salad recipe in Julia Sherman’s book Salad for President is a pleasing salad with lots of crunchy textures and punchy flavors that’s become a go-to of mine for the holidays. Thinly shaved Brussels sprouts serve as the base of the salad, while lemon-marinated, toasted almonds add bite to the equation. The dressing adds tartness with sherry and cider vinegars, which is a nice juxtaposition against the season-sweet apple pieces. Don’t skip the pickled mustard seeds if you have the time, as they add another dimension of flavor. — Dianne de Guzman, regional editor, Northern California/Pacific Northwest

This is less of an elaborate recipe, and more of a plea: Please don’t bring steamed green beans to Thanksgiving dinner (or any holiday, for that matter). They’re hardly offensive, but I’ve always found them to taste a bit ghostly and one-note. Instead, I like this simple but impactful recipe of garlicky green beans. High-heat oil, garlic, and ice cubes at-the-ready will give you crispy green beans with a welcome, garlicky char to liven up the usual parade of sweet potatoes and all the beige classics. — Francky Knapp, staff writer

I have become the Sweet Potato Bringer at our family’s large, outdoor potluck Thanksgiving, mostly because I am the only one who must have them (or it’s not Thanksgiving, obviously). Every year, I bring a sweet potato casserole with essentially the same elements: mashed sweet potatoes — slow-roasting them in the oven lends a deeper flavor — brightened with things like orange juice or cinnamon applesauce; some sort of pecan-y crumbly brown sugar topping; and blistered marshmallows. It’s all very satisfying but can become somewhat formulaic, which is why, a couple years ago, I kicked it up a notch with Epicurious’s s’moresy take on the classic: In this recipe, the sweet potato mixture gets added earthiness from maple syrup and unsweetened cocoa powder, while the pecan topping’s punch-up is the addition of crushed graham crackers (you can buy them gluten-free to be more inclusive). It’s not a dramatically different flavor from the original, meaning the eternal crowd-pleaser lives on. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager

If I am having a holiday party with a spread, The Cheese Thing will be on the table and will be decimated quickly — my repeat guests have come to expect and crave it. The Cheese Thing defies explanation; what can be said is that it’s very much a personal blog recipe, its name coined by Mitchell Davis and then surfaced more broadly on the internet by Bon Appétit back in 2018. On its surface, it just sounds like a sort of wonky baked ziti. It is the ultimate comfort recipe; cubes of cheese melt into the crevices of penne pasta, melding with a super-simple sweet and buttery tomato sauce. I absolutely shower it in salt, cracked pepper, and fluffy Pecorino, and sometimes bake extra cheese onto the top. I’d consider it a side because it lacks main-course energy and is ideal for a potluck or buffet, but there’s no doubt that it could serve as an entree on a chilly night for two, four, or however many people fit on your couch. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor

#6461. Scientists Catch Water Molecules Breaking Apart Before Their Electrons Can Respond

When X-rays strike a water molecule, the molecule can break apart faster than its electrons can complete a fundamental relaxation process. Scientists have discovered that both bonds holding hydrogen to oxygen can rupture within just a few femtoseconds, leaving behind an excited, electrically neutral oxygen atom.

The discovery challenges established interpretations of how water responds to X-ray radiation. It also identifies a previously overlooked source of highly reactive atomic oxygen, which can participate in further chemical reactions.

When a water molecule absorbs a sufficiently energetic X-ray photon, an electron can be ejected from an inner shell of its oxygen atom. The resulting vacancy normally triggers Auger decay, a rapid process in which another electron fills the vacancy and transfers enough energy to eject a second electron.

However, the researchers found that the molecular structure can change even faster. The particular electronic state produced by X-ray absorption creates strong repulsive forces, allowing both oxygen-hydrogen bonds to break before Auger decay occurs.

“What makes this result particularly exciting is that we see the molecule break apart before the electronic relaxation has even finished. Both O–H bonds rupture within the lifetime of the oxygen core hole, so the nuclear motion is essentially winning the race against the electrons,” explained Florian Trinter of FHI in Berlin.

The team examined isolated water molecules in the gas phase using high-resolution electron spectroscopy at two synchrotron facilities: PETRA III at DESY in Hamburg, Germany, and the FlexPES beamline at MAX IV in Lund, Sweden.

Both experiments detected unusually sharp peaks at specific electron energies. These features could not be explained by the electronic decay of intact water molecules or the molecular fragments typically expected after X-ray absorption.

“Seeing the characteristic signal also at MAX IV was an important part of establishing this as a genuine molecular fragmentation pathway. The measurements at the two facilities give us a very consistent picture of what happens to the water molecule after X-ray excitation,” said Gunnar Öhrwall of MAX IV in Lund.

To determine what produced the unusual electron signals, the researchers performed detailed molecular and atomic calculations. The predicted electron energies matched the decay of excited neutral oxygen atoms rather than hydroxyl (OH) fragments.

This distinction matters because the energies of emitted electrons depend on the electronic structure of the atom or molecule producing them. The exceptionally narrow spectral features provided a recognizable signature of oxygen that had already separated from the original water molecule.

“The energy of the emitted electrons provides a kind of fingerprint of the state that is formed. Our calculations show that the observed features are consistent with the decay of an excited neutral oxygen atom that has already separated from the water molecule,” explained Ludger Inhester of CFEL at DESY in Hamburg.

The results offer a new explanation for high-energy electron features observed in earlier water experiments. Signals previously associated with hydroxyl fragments may instead originate from excited neutral oxygen atoms produced through extremely rapid molecular fragmentation.

Because neutral atomic oxygen is highly reactive, understanding how it forms could improve models of chemical processes initiated by X-ray radiation. The findings also provide a more precise basis for interpreting electron spectra from water and related molecular systems.

Reference: “Ultrafast Dissociation of Water Producing Atomic Oxygen following Excitation above the O 1s Threshold” by Florian Trinter, Stephan Thürmer, Qi Zhou (周琪), Uwe Hergenhahn, Bernd Winter, Olle Björneholm, Maxim Tchaplyguine, Ludger Inhester and Gunnar Öhrwall, 5 November 2026, Physical Review Letters. DOI: 10.1103/c1hm-82p2

Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter.Follow us on Google and Google News.

Catching the heavier atomic nuclei snapping both O-H bonds within femtoseconds—before the electrons finish relaxing—shows how physical strain and structural motion can outpace electronic adjustment at the molecular scale. When X-ray excitation strips a core electron, the water molecule ejects a neutral oxygen atom before electronic decay even completes. Viewed through a Torsion Hill lens, this timing inversion offers a compelling molecular-scale parallel for torsional tension initiating structural separation and motion ahead of radiative equilibration. Standard molecular physics accounts for this directly via core-hole potential energy surfaces and ultrafast nuclear dynamics, keeping the experimental mechanism distinct and showing how the Torsion Hill conceptual framework keeps both intact. Nearly 50 years after launch, NASA's Voyager 1 probe will pass the one light-day mark on Nov. 18, a symbolic milestone for the agency's longest-running mission. Scientists reflect on the Voyager program's legacy and what comes next.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Voyager 1 probe, already the farthest human-made object in space, is about to set another record. On Nov. 18, the spacecraft will be so far from Earth that light, the universe's ultimate speed limit, takes a full 24 hours to reach it.

For researchers who worked on the Voyager program and continue to study its data, the symbolic milestone of being a full light-day from Earth celebrates a mission that continues half a century after it began. Since launching in September 1977, the twin Voyager probes have outlasted many of the engineers who built them, and their flybys of the outer solar system planets remain some of the best close-up observations scientists have of those distant worlds.

"Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 are transcending generations," Pascal Lee, a planetary scientist at the SETI Institute who was part of the Voyager 2 team at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) during its Neptune flyby in 1989, told Live Science. "Not only is their data relevant, but they themselves are still out there, moving into the unknown."

Here is what the Voyagers have revealed about the solar system and interstellar space, what happens when their power finally runs out, and whether anyone — or anything — might ever intercept the messages from Earth they carry.

A NASA simulation showing where Voyager 1 is relative to the sun and solar system planets.

Voyager 1, cruising through space at nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 km/h), is just shy of 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers) from Earth. That's the distance light travels in 24 hours, also known as one light-day. The spacecraft will reach this milestone on Nov. 18 at 5:16:07 a.m. ET, after traveling through space for 49 years, two months and 11 days.

As long as that sounds, "it's still pathetically slow in the grand scheme of things," Lee told Live Science.

If anything, it reminds us of the sheer vastness of space and time, and how this spacecraft is just a little mote of dust that's barely drifted out of the solar system still.

Scientifically speaking, Voyager 1 hasn't even left its home neighborhood yet. In 2012, the probe traveled beyond the heliosphere, the bubble of plasma blown outward by the sun that shields the planets from incoming cosmic radiation. But it still remains within the sun's gravitational grasp, which extends past the Oort Cloud — a vast spherical shell of icy bodies surrounding the solar system. Voyager 1 will need about 300 more years just to reach the cloud's inner edge, and possibly 30,000 years to fly beyond it, according to NASA.

"If anything, it reminds us of the sheer vastness of space and time, and how this spacecraft is just a little mote of dust that's barely drifted out of the solar system still," Lee said.

On its current path, Voyager 1 will pass within 1.7 light-years of a dim star called Gliese 445 in about 40,000 years, at which point it will be closer to that star than to our own sun. Farther out, the nearest star system to our own, Proxima Centauri, sits about 4.24 light-years away — more than 1,500 times farther than Voyager 1 will be on Nov. 18.

Meanwhile Voyager 1's twin, Voyager 2, took a different route through the solar system after both probes launched in 1977, in order to swing past Uranus and Neptune after revisiting Jupiter and Saturn. Currently in interstellar space about 13 billion miles (21 million km) from Earth, Voyager 2 will reach its own light-day mark in November 2035, according to NASA.

An illustration of the Voyager probes passing beyond the heliopause, into interstellar space.

Crossing the one-light-day mark doesn't change how NASA communicates with the probe, though it does demand more patience.

NASA talks to the spacecraft using radio signals, which travel at the speed of light. At a distance of one light-day, a signal sent from Earth takes 24 hours to reach Voyager 1, and a reply takes another 24 hours to make the return journey.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL, said in a recent statement.

As the spacecraft continues to cruise deeper into space, that wait will grow longer. Moreover, 50 years of traversing the solar system and the increasing distance from our sun takes a toll on the probe itself. Because sunlight in the outer reaches is far too faint for solar panels, Voyager 1 relies on nuclear batteries that convert heat from the natural decay of plutonium into electricity. That supply is gradually dwindling, prompting NASA to gradually shut down nonessential instruments to conserve what energy remains and extend the mission as much as possible.

Kelly Perry, a data systems engineer on the Voyager program at JPL, told Live Science via email that the mission team's priority remains the same: "keep the spacecraft going as long as possible."

A montage of planets imaged by the twin Voyager probes, showing Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Before the Voyagers launched, the outer solar system was largely a blur of telescopic speculation. The twin probes took advantage of a planetary alignment that comes around only once every 176 years, using the gravity of giant planets to slingshot themselves onward.

Together, they have discovered 23 moons across the outer solar system, revealed faint rings around Jupiter and captured the first detailed atmospheric profiles of Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. They also gave the first detailed, close-up views of Jupiter's moon Europa, transforming our perception of it from a blurry speck into a remarkably smooth, geologically young world — and now one of the prime candidates for finding extraterrestrial life.

We had no idea what they looked like. And all of a sudden they became places we could map, imagine ourselves exploring, landing on…they became places.

Among the more striking finds, Voyager 1 spotted active volcanoes on Jupiter's moon Io in 1979, the first time they had been seen on any world other than Earth.

"We had no idea what they looked like," Lee said. "And all of a sudden they became places we could map, imagine ourselves exploring, landing on…they became places," he added.

"That's what Voyager was for me — a voyage of discovery," he said.

These discoveries laid the groundwork for decades of follow-up exploration, including NASA's Galileo mission to Jupiter and the Cassini mission to Saturn. Decades later, as the only spacecraft to return in situ data from outside the heliosphere, the probes also proved that interstellar space is a dynamic, complex frontier rather than an empty vacuum.

Each Voyager spacecraft launched with 10 science instruments. Today, only two remain active on Voyager 1 and three on Voyager 2, measuring the magnetic fields, plasma and cosmic rays of interstellar space.

NASA began switching off the others one by one decades ago to conserve power, including the camera on Voyager 1 just minutes after it snapped the famous "Pale Blue Dot" portrait of the solar system in 1990. Ongoing power-saving reconfigurations have since helped keep the aging spacecraft operational nearly 50 years into its lifetime.

Voyager's iconic "Pale Blue Dot" image shows Earth as a "mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam," in the words of Carl Sagan.

In one such recent effort, nicknamed the "Big Bang," engineers shut off certain high-power subsystems while switching on lower-power alternatives, which "bought us almost two more years during which we will not need to turn any instrument off," Perry said.

With onboard power steadily dwindling, however, "there's a recognition that it won't be forever," Deana Weibel, an anthropologist at the Grand Valley State University in Michigan who co-authored an upcoming book about the Golden Record aboard the Voyager probes, told Live Science.

Because Voyager is a science mission, its mission will be considered finished when "no science instruments are operational," Perry said. "The Science Team decided that the last remaining instrument will be the magnetometer," she added. "We will never intentionally power off this instrument."

After the science data eventually stops, both probes may still keep beaming back basic engineering updates, such as about their health and power status, until around 2036, according to NASA. Even after the spacecraft finally fall silent, they will keep coasting through interstellar space, and "analysis shows that they should remain intact," Perry said.

Scientists will still be able to calculate their positions based on their last known speed and trajectories, Weibel said. "We'll know intellectually where it is unless it gets intercepted."

An illustration of Voyager shown next to the Golden Record.

Theoretically, yes. But interstellar space is so unfathomably vast that the chances of aliens finding the probes are vanishingly small, Lee said.

That makes it unlikely that aliens will ever find the Voyager Golden Records — twin gold-plated discs meant to portray the diversity of life on Earth. They hold sounds such as wind and animal calls, greetings in 55 languages, images of our planet and a celestial map pinpointing its location — all intended for a hypothetical civilization capable of retrieving and playing them. (The probes also carry visual instructions for spinning the records).

In that sense, the Golden Records are as much an artistic exercise as a scientific one.

"The chances of us going after Voyager 1 and bringing it back for the Smithsonian — not that it's likely — are more believable than any chance of an alien civilization finding it, and then playing the record," Lee said.

Knowing that Voyager will continue its mission long past my lifetime actually gives me comfort

If an extraterrestrial civilization did find the probe after we lost contact with it, "we would have no way of knowing," Weibel added. "It becomes something that's powered entirely by imagination at that point."

So why send a message at all? All three scientists interviewed for this story see the Golden Record as a cosmic time capsule, a symbolic gesture meant to unite humanity around a shared home planet. For all its imperfections, including the omission of some widely spoken languages and a few mislabeled tracks, the disc remains an enduring emblem of human presence on Earth, they said.

"Knowing that Voyager will continue its mission long past my lifetime actually gives me comfort," Perry told Live Science. "Although I won't be able to speak to the Voyager spacecraft any more, I love knowing that I'll always be able to look to the stars and know they're still on their way."

Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Space.com, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston. #6459. Feast Your Eyes on Uranus at Opposition This Thanksgiving 2026

Why late November 2026 is prime Uranus observing season.

The outer planets are ever so slowly starting to sneak back into the evening sky this month. First, Saturn crossed this mark last month on October 4th, then Neptune followed suit on September 26th. Now, the planet Uranus makes the transition, crossing opposition next week.

Opposition occurs on November 25th. On âU.S. Thanksgiving-eve.â We say âoppositionâ for an outer planet, as a point at which it seems to rise âoppositeâ to the setting Sun as seen from our Earthly vantage point. Orbiting the Sun at a leisurely pace once every 84 years, Uranus has a synodic period of 370 days, meaning oppositions for the planet only slide forward about five days each year. This year sees Uranus reach opposition in the astronomical constellation of Taurus, between the Hyades and the Pleiades open star clusters.

Uranus at opposition for 2026. Credit: Stellarium.

Shout out to the Full November Beaver Moon nearby on the same date as opposition 2026, fresh off of occulting the Pleiades for the Arctic on November 24th.

Uranus reached aphelion 20 Astronomical Units (AU) from the Sun in 2009, and is now inbound toward perihelion 18.3 AU distant in 2050. In 2033, Uranus will pass the point in Taurus where it was discovered by Sir William Herschel on March 13th, 1781, between the horns of the Bull very near the constellation's border with Gemini. Uranus made spurious appearances on star charts of the era at least 20 times prior to discovery.

The discovery position of Uranus. Credit: Dave Dickinson/Starry Night

Uranus reached its southernmost point in the sky in 2007, and crossed the celestial equator multiple times from 2011-2012. Uranus crosses the ecliptic plane northward in 2029. Uranus reaches its northernmost in 2032, and then begins the long trek southward. The Moon wonât resume occulting the planet Uranus again until a cycle starting on September 29th, 2029.

The Moon occults the Pleiades on November 24th. Credit: Occult 4.2.

Observing +5.5 magnitude Uranus is as easy as sweeping the suspect field at low power, and looking for a blue-green âstarâ that obstinately refuses to snap into focus. To my eye, Uranus looks like a tiny planetary nebula or perhaps a distant fuzzy comet. In fact, thatâs exactly what Herschel thought heâd first discovered, back on that fortuitous night in 1781. He later correctly realized after following the new object for several nights that it was a distant, and therefore intrinsically large object far out in the solar system beyond Saturn, then thought to mark its outer boundary. All of this happened in his backyard garden in Bath, England. We can, however, be thankful that the name âGeorgeâ that Herschel proposed to honor his benefactor King George the III didnât stick (!)

One of Herschel's speculum metal mirrors and telescopes at the London Science Museum. Credit: Dave Dickinson

Can you see Uranus with the naked eye? Topping +6th magnitude near opposition, itâs knocking on naked eye visibility from a good dark sky site. At the eyepiece, Uranus only shows a 4â disk at around opposition, barely resolvable with a telescope and tough to tease out detail.

A fine capture of Uranus from 2017. Credit: Szabolcs Nagy.

Uranus is tipped over 98 degrees (prograde) on its side, the result of some ancient encounter with another large body early in the solar systemâs history. Currently, weâre staring nearly directly at the rotational (north?) pole/hemisphere of the planet, which will be pointed nearly directly towards us in late 2029.

Though Uranus has 29 known moons, only five are within potential reach of amateur telescopes, with +13.9 magnitude Titania being the brightest. Orbiting Uranus once every 8.7 days, Titania reaches a greatest elongation of 28â from Uranus. We once saw a sharp view of the moons observing through the Steward Observatoryâs Kuiper Telescope in the Santa Catalina Mountains outside of Tucson, Arizona. They were a surprisingly easy catch through the enormous 61â telescope.

A fine capture of Uranus and its moons. Credit: Ralph Smyth.

A planetarium program such as Stellarium and Starry Night will show you the current orientation of the moons of Uranus, to help parse them out from any nearby background stars.

The orbits an orientations of the major Uranian moons. Credit: Starry Night.

The orbits of the moons are currently nearly perpendicular to our view in 2026, though theyâre edge-on and can transit Uranus as seen from our view once every 42 years. This last occurred on 2006-2009, and will happen again starting around 2048.

Hubble captures a shadow transit of Ariel in 2006. Credit: NASA/ESA/L. Sromovsky/University of Wisconsin.

Will we return to Uranus in the coming years? To date, only one mission has seen the planet close up: NASAâs Voyager 2, which flew past Uranus and its moons in 1986. Cassini-style orbiters have been proposed, though such a mission would be a lengthy affair, needing to first make the trip to the distant ice giant then slow down to enter orbit. As it stands, such a mission would be feasible for around the 2040s time frame.

JWST's view of Uranus and its rings. Credit: NASA/JWST.

Certainly, Uranus calls out for a dedicated mission. But you can explore the planet yourself tonight as it nears opposition for 2026.

David Dickinson is a freelance science writer and long-time sky watcher. He has built telescopes and observatories, chased eclipses, and travels and observes with his wife, Myscha, on a mission to get âeyes on the skyâ worldwide. His books The Universe Today Ultimate Guide to Observing the Cosmos, The Astronomerâs Deep-Sky Field Guide and science fiction short stories are available here.

#6458. Rep. Darren Soto survives Republican-drawn map in Florida

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, here at a hearing in July, has won a sixth term representing the 9th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, the most vulnerable House Democrat running for reelection, narrowly won a sixth term Tuesday in a district that state Republicans redrew in their favor.

Soto was leading Republican Navy veteran Dan Green by less than a point when The Associated Press called the race for Central Florida’s 9th District a week after Election Day. His margin of victory was above the 0.5 percent threshold that would trigger a recount under state law.

House Democrats have so far flipped more than 40 seats and appear on track to hold their biggest majority in the chamber in decades. Soto’s win means that no House Democratic incumbent lost to a Republican in the general election this year. And Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had hoped to pick up under the state’s new Republican-drawn map.

Democratic Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz both won reelection from districts that shifted red, while Democrat Pia Dandiya, a former high school principal, defeated Republican Marine Corps veteran Casey Askar for a redrawn open seat in South Florida.

Soto, who declared victory last week, had been seen as the most vulnerable of the targeted Florida Democrats. The new map reduced the Hispanic population of his district as the seat shifted from one that Kamala Harris would have carried in 2024 to one that Donald Trump would have taken by 18 points.

“Despite the Florida Republican legislature’s efforts to redraw me out of this district, my record of delivering for Florida showed voters that I am a reliable fighter for them in Congress,” Soto said in a Nov. 4 statement.

In a Tuesday memo detailing how House Democrats secured their historic majority, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee took aim at Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting efforts, saying their “attempts to steal seats … supremely backfired.”

While Florida Republicans were unsuccessful in flipping the four Democrat-held seats, the party held all of its House seats in the Sunshine State. Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar narrowly won reelection in the Miami-area 27th District over Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez, the AP reported Tuesday. In the 7th District outside Orlando, Republican former TV news anchor Ryan Elijah defeated Democratic Navy veteran Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff who conceded Tuesday.
